summary: Defines the process for registering new URL scheme names, such as the part before the colon in a web address. It is a Best Current Practice and was replaced by RFC 4395.

plainLanguage.summary: A URL scheme is the start of an address, like the label on a mailbox type. This explains how to officially claim a new label.

questions: how to register a url scheme
what is an ietf tree registration
subtitle: How to officially register a new URL scheme name.

tldr.problem: As new Internet protocols and services emerge, people need new URL scheme names (the part before the colon). Without a registration process, scheme names could collide or be created carelessly.
tldr.mechanism: This document defines a registration process with multiple registration trees: the IETF tree for general-interest schemes requiring standards-track review, and alternative trees for different needs with varying levels of scrutiny.
tldr.outcome: New URL schemes are registered in an orderly, well-specified way that prevents collisions and ensures quality. It was superseded by RFC 4395.

today: RFC 2717 has been superseded by RFC 4395, which provides updated procedures for registering new URL schemes. Current registrations should follow RFC 4395.

sections.title: Introduction and Motivation
sections.content:
A Uniform Resource Locator (URL) starts with a scheme name — the part before the colon. HTTP, FTP, mailto and many others are well-known schemes. As new Internet services and protocols emerge, new schemes become necessary. However, without a defined registration process, scheme names could conflict, and schemes could be created without adequate specification.

This document defines how to register new URL scheme names. A parallel document, RFC 2718, provides guidelines for designing URL schemes. The primary concern here is the scheme name itself and the process to register it, not the design of the scheme's semantics.
sections.plainLanguage: New internet services need new names for their addresses. This sets up a system so everyone doesn't try to use the same name.

sections.title: Registration Trees and Ownership Models
sections.content:
The document defines multiple registration trees to accommodate different needs. The IETF tree is for URL schemes of general interest to the Internet community. Schemes in this tree undergo substantive review and must be published in either a Standards Track or, in rare cases, an Informational RFC. The IETF owns schemes registered in this tree, and any changes require the same level of RFC publication as the original registration.

The document also provides a framework for alternative registration trees. These trees can have different governance models, ownership structures, and registration requirements. Each alternative tree must have a unique prefix established by a Standards Track document. For example, a company-specific tree might be called "company-schemes-" and allow scheme names like "company-schemes-custom". Alternative tree schemes do not require RFC publication but may be documented informally.

The syntax for alternative trees is: <prefix>'-'<tree-specific identifier>. This prevents name collisions between the IETF tree and any alternative trees.
sections.plainLanguage: Official schemes go through a strict review process. Company-specific or experimental schemes can use a different process with a special prefix to avoid confusion.

sections.title: Requirements for IETF Tree Registration
sections.content:
All URL schemes must conform to the generic URL syntax defined in RFC 2396. For the IETF tree specifically, several requirements apply. The scheme name MUST NOT contain a dash (hyphen) character, which is reserved to distinguish alternative tree schemes.

A security analysis is REQUIRED for all IETF tree schemes. URL schemes should not introduce additional security risks, embed confidential information like passwords, or subvert existing protocols. The specification must clearly address these concerns.

When a Standards Track RFC is used, the scheme description must address all items in the registration template: the scheme name, syntax (preferably in ABNF), character encoding considerations, intended usage, applications that use it, interoperability considerations, security analysis, relevant publications, contact information, and author/change controller details.
sections.plainLanguage: Official schemes must have a clear design, explain how they work safely, and avoid containing secrets like passwords.

sections.title: Registration and Change Control Procedures
sections.content:
For the IETF tree, the process begins with publishing an Internet-Draft describing the scheme. After at least 4 weeks of review, the draft is submitted to the IESG for evaluation. The IESG may refer it to a working group or directly hold a last-call review. Once approved, the scheme is published as an RFC and registered.

For alternative trees, the registration mechanism depends on the tree's defining document. Some alternative trees use IANA registration, others use informal mailing list announcements, and some have no formal registration at all. The change control rules also vary: IETF tree schemes can only be changed via new RFCs, while alternative tree schemes may allow the owner to make changes with varying levels of notification.

The document emphasizes that the registration mechanism must be documented and workable. If an alternative tree proposes an impractical registration mechanism, the IESG may reject the tree's definition.
sections.plainLanguage: IETF schemes go through a debate period and formal approval. Other trees can have quicker registration if they're not for wide public use.

sections.title: Security Considerations and Best Practices
sections.content:
Registration information must be authenticated to prevent fraudulent registrations. Since security vulnerabilities and best practices evolve, security documentation for registered schemes may need updating over time. New vulnerabilities should be attached to existing documentation so users are not misled.

For alternative trees delegated to parties outside the IETF, those parties should have security procedures in place to authenticate registration changes and prevent unauthorized modifications. The IESG has discretion to reject alternative tree proposals if they lack adequate security safeguards.

The document recommends that alternative tree schemes still follow the guidelines in RFC 2718 and provide security analysis. Even if a scheme is designed for limited use (such as a proprietary protocol), the security analysis should be accurate and identify all known risks.
sections.plainLanguage: Schemes need to be registered by people with authority to do so. If vulnerabilities are discovered later, they should be documented so users stay informed.
